analysis.one_liner: Blocks Medicare from testing AI-assisted prior authorization that could delay or deny care.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would stop Medicare from implementing its WISeR prior-authorization model, has been referred to two House committees and has not received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In July 2025, Medicare officials announced a test called WISeR that would require patients in traditional Medicare to get advance approval before certain services, using a process the bill's text links to artificial intelligence. This bill would bar the Health and Human Services Secretary from carrying out that model or any substantially similar one, and would permanently prohibit Medicare innovation models from testing prior authorization — including AI-based prior authorization — for services covered under Medicare Part A or Part B.
analysis.who_benefits: Older and disabled Americans in traditional Medicare, who would not face a new requirement to get advance approval for covered services, and the doctors and other providers who would otherwise have to fight those approval decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Traditional Medicare patients and their providers

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from implementing the WISeR prior-authorization model announced in the July 2025 federal register notice, or any substantially similar model.

It permanently amends the Social Security Act so Medicare innovation models cannot test prior authorization — including through artificial intelligence — for items or services paid under Medicare Part A or Part B.

analysis.who_pays: Firms that would have contracted to run prior authorization in traditional Medicare lose a new market, and the Medicare program forgoes any savings from catching unnecessary care that the model was designed to test.

drawbacks.text: The model the bill would block is formally titled the 'Wasteful and Inappropriate Services Reduction (WISeR) Model,' meaning Medicare designed it to cut spending on services it considers wasteful or inappropriate; blocking it means giving up that test.

Prior authorization can catch care that is unnecessary or harmful, so a blanket ban on testing it in traditional Medicare also rules out finding out whether it saves money for taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is protection for patients from a new approval requirement in a program that has never used prior authorization broadly, and the main cost is forgoing possible savings from reduced wasteful care. How large the savings would have been is unproven, since the model was only a test; the patient-side risk of AI-assisted denials is the concern the bill responds to.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House on December 2, 2025 and sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the bill on December 2, 2025, joined by Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
The bill has three cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained: the prior-authorization test Medicare officials announced in July 2025 remains on track while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Medicare model remains in place

for.name: Rep. Greg Landsman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit the WISeR prior-authorization model and future prior-authorization tests in traditional Medicare.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only named co-sponsor.

for.name: Two additional House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill after introduction, bringing cosponsorship to three.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and no member has acted against the bill in the record.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the market the WISeR model would have created for firms hired to run advance-approval reviews in traditional Medicare. Those vendors' revenue depends on volume of reviews, which puts their interest at odds with patients who want care approved quickly.

Providers would be spared new advance-approval paperwork and denied-payment fights for Part A and Part B services. Their interest in being paid for delivered care runs alongside patients' interest in receiving it.

analysis.trajectory: With only three cosponsors, no Republican support, and referral to two committees without any scheduled hearing, the bill is likely to sit in committee without a markup or a floor vote, as most bills at this stage do.
